messages.author: 60876d83c466f9b2
messages.subject: Time series and evolutionary models
parts:
Hey guys,


So I have a question for you.

I'm interested in characterizing the "evolutionary mode" of trajectories corresponding to shape variables on a time-continuum. My understanding from the literature is that models of continues trait evolution within a phylogenetic context are currently not accommodating for multivariate data-sets. But what about assessing the "mode" of an overall time-series based on shape-data? Can these model-fitting approaches soundly be applied as a means to ascribe a particular 'mode' to a given diversity profile (independent of a phylogeny).


I hope that made sense : )


All the best,

Mohamad

messages.subject: RE: Time series and evolutionary models
parts:
Mohamad,

 

Not sure what you mean by the mode of a trajectory. If you are implying whether trajectories change in parallel fashion, or divergently or convergently in morphospace, yes one can do this using trajectory analyses and some post-hoc tests of starting and ending points. Adams and Nistri 2010 (BMC Evol. Biol.) provides an explicit test of convergence for allometric trajectories.


Best,


Dean

messages.author: 4d71c6e24fb21497
messages.subject: RE: Time series and evolutionary models
parts:
Mohamad,


One can certainly do disparity analyses over time. One need only identify which individuals correspond to which time periods (ie, time-groups).

 

As to the rest of your query, more book-work is needed here. I may be mistaken, but I am fairly certain that off of Gene Hunt’s work was performed on univariate data. That means that the ‘X’ axis of some plot could be trait values and the ‘Y’ time, which greatly simplifies any hypothesis of identifying mode (is there a trend, is variance increasing, descreasing, is there a trend, etc.)?

 

For shape data, one of these axes is multivariate: that greatly complicates the matter. One can envision BM-simulations to try to get at the pattern; an example is in Sherratt et al. 206 Evolution ‘Trends in the sand…’.  Here we evaluated BM patterns versus BM with a directional trend in a subclade via simulations, and a particular test measure we devised to quantify the pattern that may distinguish the two.

 

Importantly, while such approaches are quite powerful, they do not rule out other alternatives that may explain the pattern (see Discussion of that paper). But such a method may provide you a path forward.

Dean

messages.author: 821967455f353d01
messages.subject: Re: [geomorph-r-package] RE: Time series and evolutionary models
parts:
Dean and Mohammed,

Gene's paleoTS package does only work on univariate data. One option (which I employed for my MS) is to apply the paleoTS models on principal components if GM data. There are reasons to suppose the first PC will reflect directional trend if it exist in your data, since that direction may show more variation than others. Another way to test for directional trends is using a regression of  time component~shape data; the results of that regression will show you the amount of variation in shape that can be attributed to a directional trend through time. 

Howeer, given the results of Gene's 2007 paper, I think it's important to really understand what the nulls you can expect are for directional selection, and whether they are worth examining. The hypothesis of directional trends through geologic time isn't very plausible--"trees don't grow to the sky", and so the question is what kinds of constraints limit evolution through long periods of times. I suspect there are scale dependencies at work that may be interesting to examine, and  

Mohammed, if you haven't already, I recommend reading up on the paleontology literature on discrete character disparity, and think about the differences between discrete and continuous characters. 

Best,
Kristopher

My understanding from the literature is that models of continues trait evolution within a phylogenetic context are currently not accommodating for multivariate data-sets. But what about assessing the "mode" of an overall time-series based on shape-data? Can these model-fitting approaches soundly be applied as a means to ascribe a particular 'mode' to a given diversity profile (independent of a phylogeny).

 

I hope that made sense : )

 

All the best,

Mohamad
